common_name: Green Giant Tomato (Large Green-When-Ripe Heirloom Beefsteak)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and stake or cage, since the vigorous indeterminate vines need support through a long season.

directions: Green Giant is a large-fruited, green-when-ripe heirloom beefsteak tomato grown for its sweet, richly flavored amber-green flesh rather than the red color most gardeners expect at harvest. Because the skin stays green to yellow-green even at full ripeness, judge readiness by a slight give under gentle thumb pressure and a faint softening or blush at the blossom end rather than by color change alone. It is best known in tomato-breeding circles as one of the two parent varieties, alongside Golden Dwarf Champion, crossed in 2005 to create the compact, gold-fruited Dwarf Sweet Sue for the Dwarf Tomato Project. Grow the sprawling indeterminate vines on a sturdy cage or stake in full sun, and pick fruit promptly once it softens, since overripe green tomatoes are easy to mistake for underripe ones and can spoil on the vine if left too long.

common_name: Dwarf Champion Tomato (19th-Century Potato-Leaf Dwarf Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; the short, rugose-leafed dwarf habit is self-supporting and needs only light staking in exposed sites.

directions: Dwarf Champion is a 19th-century American heirloom notable as one of the earliest true dwarf, potato-leaf tomato varieties grown in home gardens, predating both the modern Dwarf Tomato Project and its own later yellow-fruited sport, Golden Dwarf Champion, by roughly a century. Plants stay short and stocky with thick, rugose foliage and need little to no staking, setting round to slightly oblate, medium-sized pink-red fruit with mild, old-fashioned tomato flavor. Its compact, self-supporting genetics made it valuable breeding stock for later short-statured tomato lines long before dwarf habit became a deliberate modern breeding goal. Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, harvesting as fruit fully colors and softens slightly at the blossom end.
